headline: Great Point Rip on the Ebb: Bluefish Crash the Bait, Bonito Still a Ghost
subhead: Two weeks of watching that green flash and it still hasn't shown — but the bunker pushing into the Sound are pulling blues and bass right behind them.
body_markdown:
I was sitting off Great Point Monday morning, engine just idling, watching terns stack up over the rip on the last of the ebb — that tight, nervous hover they do right before they fold and drop. Bait was getting hammered underneath, water boiling white in patches maybe fifty yards wide. I ran up on it expecting to see that quick, chopping green flash that means bonito, or the harder, more surgical explosion that means albies. Instead it was bluefish — good ones, three to six pounds, just wrecking a pod of peanut bunker that had pushed in tight against the rip line. Not what I was hoping for, but I wasn't complaining once I got a Deadly Dick into the middle of it.

That's been the story for two weeks now. I keep expecting the first bonito of the season to show at Great Point or off Sankaty Head, and every morning I go out half-convinced this is the day. It isn't yet. But the pieces are there — the water's carrying real warmth, the bait is thick and getting pushed into tight seams by every tide change, and the temperature breaks that usually tip things off are starting to firm up out toward the Shoals. I've heard the same scouting talk out of Buzzards Bay and around the Vineyard — nothing confirmed, just guys seeing shapes they can't quite call yet. When it flips, it tends to flip fast. I wouldn't be shocked to hear the first real report out of this zone inside the next week to ten days, especially if this stable weather holds and the water keeps climbing in the low 70s inshore.

What we called correctly last week is playing out almost exactly as expected — this bluefish run is entirely about the bait. Wherever the bunker pods reform after getting pushed around by tide and wind, the blues show up within hours. Right now that's meaning the north side rips off Monomoy and the edge of Horseshoe Shoal, where bunker have been getting squeezed by current and picked apart. Bucktails and metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters, anything that throws flash — have been the ticket, worked fast through the froth. No need to overthink presentation right now; the blues aren't fussy, they're just violent.

Striped bass have settled into the pattern you'd expect for early August — they're not up chasing bait in the heat of the day, they're holding deep on structure and waiting for the light to change. Best fish have come off the Monomoy rips and around the deeper edges of Chatham inlet on the front half of the incoming, fished right at first light with eels or bunker chunks worked slow along bottom. A few guys have done well live-lining bunker over the deeper humps on Horseshoe Shoal at dusk, letting the current carry the bait naturally into the strike zone rather than working it hard. We're heading into the neap around the 5th and 6th, and that's going to soften current everywhere from the Point down to Monomoy — when that happens, the bass tend to compress onto the strongest remaining current hours and the deepest, coolest water they can find. That's the window I'd fish hardest this weekend, particularly the early morning push before the sun gets high.

Fluke have been the most dependable thing out here right now, honestly. Drifting the edges of Horseshoe Shoal and the flats off Monomoy Point in 15 to 25 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails have been putting keeper fluke in the boat consistently, with a scattering of shorts mixed in on every drift. The water's warm and stable enough that they're feeding actively through most of the tide, not just the peak of the moving water, which makes for a more forgiving day if you're short on time. If you want a bend in the rod without chasing shadows on the rips, that's where I'd start.

Looking ahead, I don't expect a dramatic shift in the next few days — the high pressure's holding, the bait's staying put, and the bluefish should keep working those same seams off Monomoy and Horseshoe Shoal as long as the bunker don't scatter. The bass game gets a little trickier as the neap sets in and current goes quiet; lighter jigs and slower presentations will matter more than they did last week. And I'll keep making the run out to Great Point and Sankaty every morning with my eyes locked on the water color, because sooner or later that first bonito is going to show, and when it does I want to be the one who sees the flash before anyone else does.
